The examples in Fig. 2 further illustrate how the same refinement suppresses misleading responses caused by appearance variations.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Overview of VerdictAD. A base detector $\mathcal{D}$ produces an anomaly map $\mathbf{M}$ and a score $s$ from the query $\mathbf{X}$ and the references $\mathcal{R}$. The frozen decision model $\mathcal{J}$ answers a reference-free and a reference-conditioned question on the whole image, giving the image logit $z$ that gates $s$ into $S$. It also answers one question per window $b_{i}$, either on a crop pair or on the full image with a red box, giving window logits $z_{i}$ that form the verification map $\mathbf{W}$ and reweight $\mathbf{M}$ into $\mathbf{M}^{\prime}$.
figures.headline: A frozen decision model answers global and per-window questions, and those answers gate the image score and reweight the anomaly map.
citing_sentences: As illustrated in Fig. 3, VerdictAD consists of a base anomaly detector and two decision-guided refinement modules, GVR and LVR.

abstract: Detecting defects in real-world industrial inspection often requires learning from only a few normal images per category. Recent few-shot anomaly detection methods have achieved strong performance by measuring feature differences between query images and normal references. However, visual differences do not always indicate genuine defects, as normal appearance variations can also produce high anomaly scores. Conversely, structural or logical anomalies may not produce strong local feature differences, making them difficult to detect. To address this limitation, we introduce VerdictAD, a training-free framework that refines existing anomaly detectors through visual decisions. Rather than replacing existing detectors, VerdictAD adopts a typed decision model to assess the query image and its local regions against a few normal references. By directly producing structured decision probabilities without text generation, the model provides complementary evidence for refining anomaly responses at different spatial scales. Building on this capability, we introduce two modules: Global Verdict Refinement (GVR) uses image-level decisions to refine the overall anomaly score, while Local Verdict Refinement (LVR) aggregates regional decisions to refine the anomaly map. Combined with a simple DINOv2-based detector, VerdictAD achieves competitive performance in one-shot and few-shot anomaly detection. More importantly, as a plug-and-play framework, it consistently improves existing anomaly detectors across MVTec AD, VisA, and MVTec LOCO AD, achieving strong results across one-shot and few-shot settings. Our code and experimental logs are publicly available at https://github.com/sgstq0811/VerdictAD-Jev-AD.

sections.body: Few-shot industrial anomaly detectors often score normal appearance variations as defects, while logical anomalies may produce weak local differences. Fig. 2 shows a juice bottle flagged for liquid colour and a breakfast box whose whole tray is highlighted. The authors propose **VerdictAD**, a training-free framework that keeps an existing detector and refines its outputs with typed decisions from a frozen model. That model returns probabilities over predefined answers without generating text. The base detector is a simple DINOv2-L method. Two modules are introduced: Global Verdict Refinement (GVR) for image-level scores and Local Verdict Refinement (LVR) for anomaly maps. The introduction says the modules reweight existing anomaly evidence without generating new responses.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Few-shot anomaly detectors often flag normal variations and may miss logical defects, so VerdictAD adds typed visual decisions to refine their scores.

sections.body: This section places the work among industrial anomaly detection methods, which include reconstruction, flow-based, feature-matching and statistical approaches evaluated on benchmarks such as MVTec AD and VisA. Few-shot methods include nearest-neighbour matching, AnomalyDINO, which uses patch-level DINOv2 features, FastRecon, and SubspaceAD, which fits a normal feature subspace. Vision-language methods such as WinCLIP and PromptAD adapt prompts or language-aligned representations. Typed decision models return probabilities over predefined answers instead of free text, and prior work applies them to verification, alignment, robustness and reinforcement learning. The authors state that these models remain largely unexplored for industrial anomaly detection, which is the gap VerdictAD addresses.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior few-shot methods mostly change feature representations or use vision-language prompts, while typed decision models remain unexplored for anomaly detection.

sections.body: The base detector extracts patch features from a frozen DINOv2-L encoder, takes nearest-neighbour distances to reference patches to form an anomaly map, and max-pools that map for the image score. GVR asks the frozen decision model two binary questions, one on the query alone and one with tiled references, and averages the two logits z. The image score is then gated as $S=s\cdot\sigma(z)^{\alpha}$, where sigma is the sigmoid and alpha controls the strength. LVR places 16 overlapping windows, judges each window with a crop pair and with a red-boxed full image, and averages the probabilities into a verification map W. The anomaly map is multiplied by W, so zero responses stay zero and no new anomaly evidence is created.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: VerdictAD multiplies existing anomaly scores and maps by probabilities from a frozen typed decision model, without changing the base detector.

sections.body: Experiments use MVTec AD, VisA and MVTec LOCO AD with one, two or four randomly selected normal references per category, repeated over three seeds. Metrics are image-level and pixel-level AUROC, AUPR and AUPRO, reported as percentages. The frozen decision model is the 9B-parameter Clef-Flash, with alpha set to 0.5 and gamma set to 0.25. In Table 2, four-shot image-level results on LOCO rise for PatchCore from 67.4 to 78.0 and for SubspaceAD from 67.5 to 75.3. Table 1 reports competitive performance against prior few-shot methods on MVTec AD and VisA. Applied to PatchCore, DINOv2-L, AnomalyDINO and SubspaceAD, the refinement improves image-level and pixel-level AUROC on all evaluated datasets and settings. Table 3 reports zero-shot gains for AnomalyCLIP and AdaCLIP. The paper notes that different base detectors perform best on different metrics.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Refinement lifts image-level scores on MVTec LOCO AD at four shots, for example PatchCore rising from 67.4 to 78.0.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that VerdictAD is a training-free framework that uses typed visual decisions to refine existing anomaly detectors without learning new anomaly representations. It introduces GVR to improve image-level discrimination and LVR to suppress misleading pixel-level responses. The authors report strong performance across few-shot settings and consistent gains over several detection backbones, particularly for logical anomalies. The stated limit is that the approach cannot recover anomaly evidence entirely absent from the original detector. The method adds no training step, and the authors present it as a simple way to improve existing predictions.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion finds the gains strongest for logical anomalies, but refinement cannot recover evidence absent from the base detector.
